quiz_title: Computational Thinking · Quiz 1 · 2023 Oct · Qualifier QPQ2 · Part 1
subject: Computational Thinking

prompt.value: Match the following expressions on the left with the appropriate values on the right. Match each expression to its value Expression Value a. 2 == 2 or 2 > 3 1. Invalid expression b. 2 == 2 and 2 > 3 2. True c. 2 = 3 3. False d. 2 + 2 4. 4 e. '2' < 3 5. '22'

explanation.value: a) True or False = True (2). b) True and False = False (3). c) '2 = 3' assigns to a literal — invalid (1). d) 2 + 2 = 4 (4). e) '2' < 3 compares a string with an integer — invalid (1).

prompt.value: The given procedure is executed using the "Library" dataset (Table 1). selected("Narayan", "Fiction", 10) will

options.value: At least 10 percent of the books written by Narayan are in the genre Fiction.
At most 10 percent of the books written by Narayan are in the genre Fiction.
At least 10 of the books written by Narayan are in the genre Fiction.
At most 10 of the books written by Narayan are in the genre Fiction.

explanation.value: It returns True when countG / countT <= 10 / 100, i.e. when at most 10 percent of Narayan's books are in the genre Fiction.

prompt.value: miniSum accepts three numbers as parameters and returns the sum of the two least parameters. Choose the correct code fragment to complete the procedure.

explanation.value: The first if handles A being largest (Sum = B + C). Option 4 then sets Sum = A + B whenever A is not largest, and overwrites it with A + C only when B is the largest (B > C and B > A); when C is largest the if is false and Sum stays A + B. This gives the two-smallest sum in every case. Option 1 picks A + C when C is largest (wrong), Option 2 lacks the else and overwrites the A-largest case, and Option 3 is malformed.

prompt.value: The given pseudocode is executed using a dataset with the same fields as "Words", containing the words of: "how much wood would a woodchuck chuck if a woodchuck could chuck wood". Choose the correct paragraph formed from Table 2 at the end of execution.

options.value: how much wood would a woodchuck chuck if could
how much would a woodchuck chuck if a woodchuck could chuck
how much would a woodchuck chuck if a woodchuck could chuck wood
how much would if a woodchuck could chuck wood

explanation.value: Each kept word removes its later duplicates. Removing the repeated 'a', 'woodchuck', 'chuck' and 'wood' leaves the first occurrences in order: "how much wood would a woodchuck chuck if could".

prompt.value: A company collected the data below (Table 1): for each city, the number of people willing to attend a promotion on Saturday and Sunday. The procedure bestDay(Z) is used. Which of the following is correct?
Table 1 Seq. N Source City Saturday Sunday 1 Fastabook Chennai 20 30 2 Pantagram Mumbai 50 30 3 Twitter Chennai 30 20 4 Pantagram Lucknow 30 50 5 Twitter Hyderabad 30 10 6 Fastabook Lucknow 20 50

options.value: bestDay("Lucknow") = "Sunday", bestDay("Chennai") = "Sunday"
bestDay("Lucknow") = "Saturday", bestDay("Chennai") = "Sunday"
bestDay("Lucknow") = "Sunday", bestDay("Chennai") = "Saturday"
bestDay("Lucknow") = "Saturday", bestDay("Chennai") = "Saturday"

explanation.value: Lucknow: Saturday = 50, Sunday = 100 → 100 > 50 → Sunday. Chennai: Saturday = 50, Sunday = 50; the test is the strict countSun > countSat, and 50 > 50 is false → Saturday. So Lucknow = Sunday, Chennai = Saturday.

prompt.value: The following pseudocode is executed using the "Words" dataset. What will Count represent at the end of execution?

options.value: Number of words in which the same consonant occurs consecutively exactly once
Number of words in which the same consonant occurs consecutively at least once
Number of words in which the same consonant occurs consecutively exactly twice
Number of words in which the same consonant occurs consecutively at least twice

explanation.value: C is set to 1 whenever a consonant equals the immediately preceding (consonant) letter. Since C is only ever set (never counted), it flags whether the same consonant occurs consecutively at least once in the word; Count tallies such words.

prompt.value: Swara has a variable max to find the maximum total score using the "Scores" dataset. There are many ways to initialize max. Choose the correct option(s). It is a Multiple Select Question (MSQ).

options.value: Pick any random card X from the dataset and max = X.Total
Pick the top card X from the dataset and max = X.Total
Initialize max with any random value
Initialize max with any value greater than the possible maximum total score

explanation.value: A maximum search must start from an actual value (or any value at or below the true maximum). Seeding max with a real Total (any card or the top card) is safe. An arbitrary random value may exceed every real score, and a value above the maximum certainly will, so neither can be guaranteed to update — both are wrong.
